programme.title: Prison Songs
programme.desc: The inmates of a Darwin prison are shown in a completely new light in Australia’s first ever documentary musical Prison Songs, as they share their feelings, faults and experiences in an extraordinary way – through song. Darwin Correctional Centre is the largest correctional centre in the Northern Territory. Originally designed to hold 115 prisoners when it opened in 1979, by 2014 it is overcrowded and bursting with more than 800 male and female inmates. 80% of the prisoners here are Indigenous Australians. Granted unprecedented access to film inside Berrimah before its decommission in late 2014, Prison Songs offers a rare glimpse into life in a contemporary Australian prison. (Commissioned by SBS) (Documentary) M(L) CC

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: Prison Songs
programme.desc: The inmates of a Darwin prison are shown in a completely new light in Australia’s first ever documentary musical Prison Songs, as they share their feelings, faults and experiences in an extraordinary way – through song. Darwin Correctional Centre is the largest correctional centre in the Northern Territory. Originally designed to hold 115 prisoners when it opened in 1979, by 2014 it is overcrowded and bursting with more than 800 male and female inmates. 80% of the prisoners here are Indigenous Australians. Granted unprecedented access to film inside Berrimah before its decommission in late 2014, Prison Songs offers a rare glimpse into life in a contemporary Australian prison. programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point

Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: Prison Songs
programme.desc: The inmates of a Darwin prison are shown in a completely new light in Australia’s first ever documentary musical Prison Songs, as they share their feelings, faults and experiences in an extraordinary way – through song. Darwin Correctional Centre is the largest correctional centre in the Northern Territory. Originally designed to hold 115 prisoners when it opened in 1979, by 2014 it is overcrowded and bursting with more than 800 male and female inmates. 80% of the prisoners here are Indigenous Australians. Granted unprecedented access to film inside Berrimah before its decommission in late 2014, Prison Songs offers a rare glimpse into life in a contemporary Australian prison. programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point

Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

Darwin Correctional Centre is the largest correctional centre in the Northern Territory. Originally designed to hold 115 prisoners when it opened in 1979, by 2014 it is overcrowded and bursting with more than 800 male and female inmates. 80% of the prisoners here are Indigenous Australians. Granted unprecedented access to film inside Berrimah before its decommission in late 2014, Prison Songs offers a rare glimpse into life in a contemporary Australian prison. programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: How To Get Ahead In Advertising

programme.title: Marie's Story

What follows is a brutal, darkly entertaining battle of survival, revenge and determination against impossible odds.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.desc: The inmates of a Darwin prison are shown in a completely new light in Australia’s first ever documentary musical Prison Songs, as they share their feelings, faults and experiences in an extraordinary way – through song. Darwin Correctional Centre is the largest correctional centre in the Northern Territory. Originally designed to hold 115 prisoners when it opened in 1979, by 2014 it is overcrowded and bursting with more than 800 male and female inmates. 80% of the prisoners here are Indigenous Australians. Granted unprecedented access to film inside Berrimah before its decommission in late 2014, Prison Songs offers a rare glimpse into life in a contemporary Australian prison. programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

Thanks to comparative archaeology - using images of monuments' remains from the same period - it is now possible to imagine how even heavily damaged buildings looked like at the time down to the most minute of details.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.

programme.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback
programme.desc: Episode 3 examines the legal, political and public battle that follows Kumanjayi Walker’s death, culminating in the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. Through police statements, body-worn camera footage and witness testimony, the episode revisits the events inside House 511 and focuses on the central question at the heart of the case: whether Rolfe’s second and third shots were a reasonable response to a perceived threat to his partner’s life. In the days after the shooting, Rolfe is removed from active duty and supported by colleagues and the Northern Territory Police Association. Concerns are raised about police officers connected to the incident gathering together before providing formal accounts, while public attention intensifies as Rolfe’s identity becomes widely known. Four days after Walker’s death, detectives arrest Rolfe and charge him with murder. In Yuendumu, the charge is welcomed as a sign that the death is being taken seriously, while the growing Justice for Walker campaign continues to demand accountability. At the same time, supporters rally behind Rolfe, portraying him as an officer who acted in self-defence. As the case is delayed by preliminary hearings and the COVID-19 pandemic, wider events, including the global Black Lives Matter movement, place Walker’s death within a broader discussion about race, policing and Aboriginal deaths in custody. Competing campaigns transform both Walker and Rolfe into symbols of larger social and political debates. When the trial finally begins in Darwin in 2022, longstanding concerns about fairness and representation come into focus. Family members question a jury that contains no Aboriginal people and observe courtroom arrangements that they believe favour Rolfe. The prosecution argues that while the first shot was justified, the two fatal shots fired 2.6 seconds later were not. The defence maintains that Rolfe was following police training and believed his partner remained under threat from Walker, who was armed with scissors. Body-worn camera footage becomes the central piece of evidence as competing versions of events are tested in court. Disputes emerge over whether police lawfully entered the house, the level of danger faced by officers and Rolfe’s claim that Walker attempted to reach for his firearm. Evidence relating to Rolfe’s previous conduct is excluded, further fuelling debate about what the jury is allowed to hear. The episode concludes as the case is handed to the jury. With Walker’s family seeking justice and Rolfe maintaining that his actions were lawful and necessary, the trial becomes a defining test of accountability, policing and race relations in Australia. A final preview points to the coronial inquest, where additional evidence and allegations not heard during the criminal trial will later emerge.

programme.title: The Point
programme.desc: Explores the evolving relationship between the Yuendumu community and the Northern Territory police in the lead-up to Kumanjayi Walker's death, its immediate aftermath, and the community’s experience seven years on. Through the perspectives of Uncle Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves the episode considers the impact of these events and how they continue to shape the community today.
